lessons.title: Heat Damage: Prevention and Repair
lessons.body:
Heat damage happens when the temperature of your tool is too high for your hair type, or when you use heat too often without protection. In natural hair, the bonds that give curls their shape can be permanently broken by temperatures above 450Â°F (232Â°C). Once that happens, the hair will not curl back, even when wet. In Africa, many women use heat tools without a heat protectant because they are not easily available or seem expensive. But a simple heat protectant spray or serum costs about the same as a loaf of bread and can save your hair. Always check the temperature setting on your tool. For fine or damaged hair, stay below 300Â°F (150Â°C). For normal hair, 350Â°F (175Â°C) is safe. For coarse, resistant hair, you can go up to 400Â°F (205Â°C) but never higher. If your tool has no temperature control, do not use it on natural hair.

Prevention is easier than repair. Before any heat styling, wash and deep condition your hair. Apply a leave-in conditioner and then a heat protectant. Section your hair into small parts, no more than 1 inch thick. Never use heat on wet hair unless you are blow-drying with a dryer designed for it. A common mistake is to pass the flat iron over the same section many times. Two passes are enough. If the hair does not straighten after two passes, your tool is not hot enough or your sections are too big. Also, limit heat styling to once every two weeks. Give your hair a rest between sessions.

If you already have heat damage, you cannot fully repair it. The damaged hair must grow out. But you can manage it. First, stop all heat use for at least 3 months. Trim the most damaged endsâabout 1 to 2 inchesâbecause split ends travel up the hair shaft. Deep condition every week with a protein treatment followed by a moisturizing deep conditioner. Use a plastic cap and sit under a hooded dryer for 20 minutes, or wrap a warm towel around your head for 30 minutes. Avoid combing dry hair; always detangle with conditioner in the shower. Apply a leave-in conditioner and seal with shea butter or coconut oil. Protective styles like braids, twists, or cornrows help hide damage and protect ends. In 6 to 12 months, your natural curl pattern will return in the new growth. Be patient and consistent.

lessons.title: Using Heat Tools Safely
lessons.body:
Heat tools include blow dryers, flat irons, curling irons, and hot combs. Each has a safe temperature range. A blow dryer with a comb attachment should be used on low or medium heat (not high). Flat irons and curling irons should have adjustable temperature settings. In many African markets, you can buy a good ceramic flat iron for 3,000 to 8,000 naira (or equivalent). Avoid very cheap tools that have only on/off switchesâthey often reach 450Â°F or more and will burn your hair. Look for tools with a digital display and a temperature dial. Ceramic or tourmaline plates are better than metal because they heat evenly and cause less damage. Titanium plates heat up fast but can be too hot for fine hair.

Before you plug in any tool, do these three things: First, check the cord for cracks or exposed wires. Second, make sure your hands are dry. Third, have a heat protectant and a comb ready. Never use heat tools on wet hair unless the tool is specifically a blow dryer. Water and electricity are dangerous. Also, never leave a hot tool unattended. After use, unplug it and let it cool on a heat-resistant mat or ceramic plateânever on your bed or plastic surface.

When using a flat iron or curling iron, always start with clean, dry, fully detangled hair. Section hair into 1-inch parts. Clamp the iron near the roots and glide down smoothly, without stopping. Do not hold the iron in one spot for more than 2 seconds. For curling, wrap the hair around the barrel and hold for 5 to 8 seconds, then release. Always point the iron downward to keep the cuticle smooth. If you hear a sizzling sound or see smoke, your tool is too hot or your hair is not completely dry. Stop immediately. Let the tool cool down or dry your hair more.

Clean your tools after every use. Wipe the plates with a damp cloth (not wet) after they have cooled. Remove product buildup with a little rubbing alcohol on a cotton pad. Store tools in a dry place, not in the bathroom where steam can damage them. Check the temperature setting every timeâdo not assume it is still on the same setting. Finally, give your hair a break. Do not use heat tools more than once a week. If you must, use the lowest effective temperature and always use a heat protectant.

lessons.title: Blow-Drying Natural Hair
lessons.body:
Blow-drying is the first step to straightening natural hair. But done wrong, it can cause heat damage, breakage, and dryness. The goal is to stretch the hair without cooking it. Start with clean, deep-conditioned hair. Apply a leave-in conditioner and a heat protectant serum. Divide hair into 4 to 6 sections. Use clips to keep sections apart. Work on one section at a time. For each section, detangle with a wide-tooth comb from ends to roots. Then, apply a small amount of heat protectant again.

Use a blow dryer with a concentrator nozzle and a comb attachment. Set the dryer to low or medium heat and medium speed. High heat will burn the hair; high speed will tangle it. Hold the dryer 6 to 8 inches away from the hair. Start at the roots and move down to the ends. Move the dryer constantlyâdo not hold it in one spot. Use the comb attachment to pull the hair straight as you dry. For thicker sections, you may need to dry in smaller subsections. A full head can take 30 to 45 minutes. Do not rush. If your arms get tired, take a break. Rushing leads to tangles and uneven drying.

An alternative method is the tension method. Hold the hair taut with one hand and aim the dryer down the hair shaft with the other. This gives a smoother finish. Another method is banding: wrap sections with elastic bands (not too tight) and dry under a hooded dryer for 30 minutes, then finish with a blow dryer. In Africa, many salons use a hooded dryer after applying a setting lotion. That works too, but the hair must be completely dry before you flat iron.

After blow-drying, the hair should be stretched but not bone-dry. It should feel soft, not crispy. If it feels crispy, you used too much heat or not enough protectant. Let the hair cool completely before flat ironing. Never blow-dry wet hair with a flat iron. Also, do not blow-dry on the highest setting just to save time. It will cause irreversible damage. Clean your blow dryer's filter every month to keep it working efficiently. Store it in a dry place. If you blow-dry regularly, invest in a good quality dryer with adjustable heat and speed. A cheap dryer with only high heat will damage your hair over time.

lessons.title: Flat Ironing and Curling Techniques
lessons.body:
Flat ironing gives sleek, straight hair. Curling adds bounce and shape. Both require dry, stretched hair. Start with blow-dried hair that is 100% dry. Apply a small amount of heat protectant serum to each section before you flat iron. Set your flat iron to the right temperature: 300Â°F (150Â°C) for fine or damaged hair, 350Â°F (175Â°C) for normal hair, and up to 400Â°F (205Â°C) for coarse, resistant hair. Never exceed 400Â°F. Let the iron heat up fully. Wipe the plates with a dry cloth if there is any residue.

Section hair into 1-inch parts. Use a rat-tail comb to separate each part. Clip the rest of the hair out of the way. Take one section and comb it through from roots to ends. Clamp the flat iron near the roots, then glide it down smoothly to the ends. Do not stop or pause. Two passes are enough. If the hair is not straight after two passes, your sections are too big or the iron is not hot enough. Do not keep passing the iron over the same spot. That burns the hair. For a bump at the ends, turn the iron slightly as you reach the ends. For a sleek finish, follow with a small amount of serum or oil on your palms and smooth over the hair.

For curling, use a curling iron with a barrel size of 1 inch to 1.5 inches. Smaller barrels give tighter curls; larger barrels give loose waves. Wrap a 1-inch section of hair around the barrel, starting from the mid-lengths and leaving the ends out. Hold for 5 to 8 seconds. Release and let the curl cool in your hand or pin it with a clip. Do not pull the curl downâthat will make it drop. For a natural look, alternate the direction of the curls. For a more polished look, curl all in the same direction. Always point the iron downward. If you want to curl your hair without heat, use flexi rods or perm rods on damp hair and let it air dry or sit under a hooded dryer.

After styling, do not touch your hair until it cools completely. Then apply a light oil like argan or jojoba to add shine and reduce frizz. Do not use heavy oils or buttersâthey will weigh down the style. To make the style last, wrap your hair at night with a silk scarf or satin bonnet. Sleep on a satin pillowcase. Avoid humidityâif you live in a humid area, use a anti-humidity spray. When you are ready to wash, detangle gently with conditioner. Never rip through tangles. If you used a lot of product, clarify with a sulfate shampoo once, then deep condition.

lessons.title: Natural Hair Coloring Basics
lessons.body:
Coloring natural hair can be fun, but it can also cause dryness and breakage if done wrong. There are three main types of color: permanent, semi-permanent, and temporary. Permanent color lifts the cuticle and deposits color inside the hair. It contains ammonia and peroxide, which can be harsh. Semi-permanent color coats the outside of the hair and washes out in 6 to 12 washes. It has no ammonia and is gentler. Temporary color is like a spray or chalk that washes out in one wash. For natural hair, semi-permanent or temporary color is safer. If you want permanent color, go to a professional who understands natural hair. Do not use box dye from the supermarket without doing a strand test.

Before coloring, do a patch test on a small section of hair behind your ear. Wait 48 hours to check for allergic reactions. Also do a strand test to see how your hair reacts. Wash your hair with a clarifying shampoo to remove buildup. Do not use conditioner before coloringâit can block the color. Apply a barrier cream (like petroleum jelly) along your hairline to prevent staining your skin. Wear old clothes and gloves. Mix the color according to the instructions. Apply to dry, detangled hair. Start at the roots if you are covering gray, or at the mid-lengths if you are going lighter. Work in sections. Do not leave the color on longer than the instructions say. Rinse with cool water until the water runs clear. Then shampoo and deep condition.

After coloring, your hair will be drier than usual. You must deep condition every week for the first month. Use a protein treatment two weeks after coloring to rebuild strength. Avoid heat styling for at least two weeks. Use a sulfate-free shampoo and a rich conditioner. Seal in moisture with a leave-in conditioner and a natural oil like olive or coconut oil. Do not use products with alcohol, which will dry out the color-treated hair. If you want to lighten your hair, do not use bleach at home. Bleach can melt your hair. Go to a salon that uses gentle lighteners and knows how to protect natural hair.

In Africa, many women use henna or indigo as natural alternatives. Henna gives a reddish-brown color and also strengthens the hair. Indigo gives blue-black. You can mix them to get different shades. But henna can loosen your curl pattern over time. Always do a strand test. Also, do not use henna if you have permanent color in your hairâit can cause a bad reaction. If you are not sure, wait and save up for a professional colorist. Coloring natural hair is not a DIY project for beginners. A bad color job can cost more to fix than a good salon visit.

lessons.title: Aftercare for Heat-Styled or Colored Hair
lessons.body:
After you heat-style or color your hair, it needs extra care. Heat and chemicals strip moisture from the hair. Your job is to put moisture back and protect the hair from further damage. For the first week after coloring or heat styling, avoid washing your hair too soon. Wait at least 3 days before washing colored hair to let the color set. For heat-styled hair, you can wash after 5 to 7 days. When you wash, use a sulfate-free shampoo. Sulfates strip color and dry out heat-styled hair. Follow with a deep conditioner. Leave it on for 20 to 30 minutes with a plastic cap. If you have a hooded dryer, sit under it on low heat for 15 minutes. Otherwise, wrap a warm towel around your head.

After washing, apply a leave-in conditioner and a heat protectant if you plan to heat style again. But try to give your hair a break from heat for at least two weeks. Use protective styles like braids, twists, or buns to hide your ends and keep moisture in. Moisturize your hair every other day with a water-based leave-in conditioner. Seal with a light oil like jojoba or grapeseed. For colored hair, use a color-safe leave-in. Avoid heavy butters, which can fade color. Also, avoid chlorinated water and salt water. If you swim, wet your hair with clean water and apply a leave-in conditioner before entering the pool or ocean. Wear a swim cap.

At night, wrap your hair with a silk scarf or satin bonnet. This reduces friction and keeps moisture in. Sleep on a satin pillowcase if you can. For heat-styled hair, you can pineapple your hair (gather it in a loose ponytail on top of your head) to keep curls. For colored hair, avoid tight hairstyles that pull on the roots. Be gentle when detangling. Use a wide-tooth comb or your fingers. Start from the ends and work up. Never rip through tangles. If you find split ends, trim them. Trimming every 8 to 12 weeks keeps your hair healthy.

Watch for signs of damage: dryness, brittleness, breakage, split ends, and loss of curl pattern. If you see these, stop all heat and chemical treatments. Do a protein treatment followed by a moisturizing deep conditioner. Repeat every two weeks until the hair feels stronger. If the damage is severe, cut off the damaged ends. Remember, hair grows about 0.5 inches per month. With good aftercare, your hair will recover. Drink plenty of water, eat a balanced diet with protein and vitamins, and get enough sleep. Healthy hair starts from within. Be patient and consistent. Your hair will thank you.

quiz.q: What is the maximum safe temperature for flat ironing coarse, resistant natural hair?
quiz.explanation: Coarse, resistant hair can handle up to 400Â°F, but never higher, to avoid permanent damage.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of heat damage?
options: A) Hair curls back when wet
B) Hair feels soft and moisturized
C) Hair does not curl back when wet
quiz.explanation: When heat damage occurs, the bonds that create curls are broken, so the hair remains straight even when wet.

quiz.q: How often should you use heat tools on natural hair at most?
quiz.explanation: Limiting heat styling to once every two weeks gives hair time to recover and prevents cumulative damage.

quiz.q: What should you do before using a heat protectant?
options: A) Wash and deep condition hair
C) Use heat on wet hair
quiz.explanation: Clean, deep-conditioned hair provides a healthy base and allows the heat protectant to work effectively.

quiz.q: How many passes of a flat iron are usually enough to straighten a section?
quiz.explanation: Two passes are sufficient; more passes increase the risk of heat damage without better results.

quiz.q: What should you do if you hear a sizzling sound while flat ironing?
quiz.explanation: Sizzling means the hair is not completely dry or the tool is too hot, which can cause severe damage.

quiz.q: Which type of flat iron plates is recommended for natural hair?
quiz.explanation: Ceramic and tourmaline plates heat evenly and cause less damage than metal or aluminum.

quiz.q: How should you clean your flat iron after use?
options: B) Wipe with a damp cloth after cooling
quiz.explanation: Wiping with a damp cloth after the tool has cooled removes product buildup without damaging the plates.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to hold a blow dryer when drying natural hair?
quiz.explanation: Holding the dryer 6 to 8 inches away prevents overheating and allows even drying.

quiz.q: Which blow dryer setting is best for natural hair?
quiz.explanation: Medium heat and medium speed balance drying efficiency with safety for natural hair.

quiz.q: What is the tension method in blow-drying?
options: B) Holding hair taut while aiming dryer down the shaft
C) Drying with a hooded dryer
quiz.explanation: The tension method involves holding hair taut and aiming the dryer downward for a smoother finish.

quiz.q: How long should you wait after blow-drying before flat ironing?
options: C) Until hair is completely cool
quiz.explanation: Hair must be completely cool before flat ironing to avoid heat damage and ensure the style sets.

quiz.q: What is the recommended barrel size for loose waves?
quiz.explanation: A larger barrel like 1.5 inches creates loose waves, while smaller barrels give tighter curls.

quiz.q: How long should you hold a curling iron on a section of hair?
quiz.explanation: 5 to 8 seconds is enough to set the curl without causing heat damage.

quiz.q: What should you do after releasing a curl from a curling iron?
options: B) Let it cool in your hand or pin it
quiz.explanation: Letting the curl cool without pulling helps it hold its shape longer.

quiz.q: Which type of hair color is gentlest on natural hair?
quiz.explanation: Temporary color washes out in one wash and does not lift the cuticle, so it is the gentlest.

quiz.q: What should you do before applying permanent hair color?
options: B) Do a patch and strand test
quiz.explanation: Patch and strand tests check for allergic reactions and how your hair will respond to the color.

quiz.q: How long should you wait after coloring to wash your hair?
quiz.explanation: Waiting at least 3 days allows the color to set properly and reduces fading.

quiz.q: What natural ingredient can be used as a hair color alternative?
quiz.explanation: Henna is a natural plant dye that gives reddish-brown color and can strengthen hair.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid bleach at home on natural hair?
options: B) It can melt or severely damage hair
quiz.explanation: Bleach is a harsh chemical that can cause irreversible damage, including melting the hair.

quiz.q: How often should you deep condition colored hair in the first month?
quiz.explanation: Colored hair is drier, so weekly deep conditioning is necessary to restore moisture.

quiz.q: What should you use to wash color-treated hair?
quiz.explanation: Sulfate-free shampoo is gentler and helps preserve color for longer.

quiz.q: What is a protective style for after heat styling?
quiz.explanation: Braids or twists protect ends and retain moisture without heat or tension.

quiz.q: How often should you moisturize heat-styled or colored hair?
quiz.explanation: Moisturizing every other day keeps hair hydrated and prevents breakage.

quiz.q: What should you wear at night to protect your hair?
options: B) Silk scarf or satin bonnet
quiz.explanation: Silk or satin reduces friction and helps retain moisture in the hair.

quiz.q: What is a sign that you need a protein treatment?
options: A) Hair feels soft and stretchy
B) Hair feels mushy and breaks easily
quiz.explanation: Mushy, weak hair indicates loss of protein structure and needs a protein treatment.

quiz.q: How often should you trim heat-styled or colored hair?
quiz.explanation: Trimming every 8 to 12 weeks removes split ends and keeps hair healthy.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see split ends?
quiz.explanation: Trimming split ends prevents them from traveling up the hair shaft and causing more damage.

quiz.q: What is the best way to detangle heat-styled or colored hair?
options: A) Use a fine-tooth comb on dry hair
B) Use a wide-tooth comb or fingers from ends to roots
quiz.explanation: Gentle detangling from ends to roots with a wide-tooth comb or fingers minimizes breakage.

quiz.q: What internal factor contributes to healthy hair growth?
quiz.explanation: Hydration and a balanced diet support hair growth from within.
